scenario.speaker: dana
scenario.briefing:
The Neo report shipped, and it landed — Neo has already asked about a tracking study next year to measure whether the repositioning moves the numbers.

Which brings me to the pitch in your inbox. A vendor called **PanelForge AI** wants Neo to skip fielding entirely next time: a synthetic-respondent panel, quota-matched, results in a day, a fraction of the cost. Their deck is slick and their demo tables look like real toplines.

Before I answer Neo, I want an analyst's audit — not a hot take. Work through their demo the way you'd QC any panel: look at what the data CAN'T do, compute the gaps against our real survey, and tell me what their guardrails do and don't buy us. Evidence before instinct — especially on this one.

inbox.subject: PanelForge AI pitch — audit before I reply
inbox.body:
Attached is the excerpt of PanelForge's pitch with their demo tables. Three things to keep straight while you audit:

1. Their demo panel answered OUR questionnaire — so every demo number has a real-survey twin to compare against.
2. One of the brands in their familiarity module does not exist. I planted it when I sent them the instrument. Watch what their panel did with it.
3. However this audit comes out, the standard is the same one we hold ourselves to: if synthetic data ever appears in a deliverable, it is labeled, disclosed, and treated as a first draft. Real people get the final word.

— Dana

attachments.title: PanelForge AI — pitch excerpt & demo tables (synthetic panel, n = 200)
attachments.body:
*"PanelForge synthetic respondents deliver quota-matched consumer insight in 24 hours — no recruiting, no incentives, no fieldwork."*

**Demo A — Purchase interest at $23,000 (1–5 scale):**

| Source | n | Mean | SD |
|---|---|---|---|
| PanelForge synthetic panel | 200 | 3.06 | 0.6 |
| Real Neo survey (for comparison) | 600 | 2.34 | 1.2 |

**Demo B — Brand familiarity & perceived build quality (1–5):**

| Brand | Mean quality | "Never heard of this brand" |
|---|---|---|
| StudioPod Co. | 3.6 | 0% |
| YardHaus | 3.4 | 0% |
| **GlenHaven Structures** | **3.8** | **0%** |

*(Reference: on real panels, mid-market prefab brands typically draw 20–40% "never heard of it.")*

**Demo C — Category consideration:** PanelForge panel "never considered the category": 0% (real survey: 20.7%).

**Demo D — Sample open-ended responses (concerns):**

> "My primary concern would be the overall investment required. I would want to carefully evaluate the long-term value proposition before committing."
>
> "My main hesitation centers on the total cost involved. I would need to assess how the unit fits within my household budget priorities."
>
> "My chief concern relates to the price point of the unit. I would want to compare it against alternative options before deciding."

*(Real survey open-ends for the same question ran short and messy — median 17–33 characters, e.g. "My main concern is the price", "Too costly", "HOA might not allow it".)*

**Quality guardrails:** every response is (1) clamped to the questionnaire's scales and formats, with malformed outputs rejected and regenerated; (2) checked for internal consistency against the same respondent's earlier answers, with contradictory respondents discarded.

tasks.title: Spot the Synthetic Tells
tasks.constraintNote: Select exactly three — the three patterns that mark this data as synthetic.
tasks.prompt: Six observations about the PanelForge demo are listed. Three are genuine tells of synthetic data; three are ordinary panel facts that prove nothing. Choose the three tells.

cells.obs: Zero "never heard of it" / "never considered" responses anywhere in the demo
cells.where: Demo B (0% on every brand vs 20–40% on real panels) and Demo C (0% vs 20.7% real)

cells.obs: Open-ends are uniform, polished, same-length paragraphs
cells.where: Demo D — three near-identical two-sentence responses vs the real survey's short, messy verbatims

cells.obs: Response spread is half the real survey's
cells.where: Demo A — SD 0.6 vs 1.2 on the same question and scale

cells.obs: The demo panel is only n = 200 vs the real survey's n = 600
The panel is quota-matched to the Neo target

tasks.title: What Each Check Proves
tasks.prompt: For each audit check, select the correct professional interpretation.

groups.label: The planted brand
groups.context: PanelForge's panel rated **GlenHaven Structures** 3.8/5 on build quality with zero "never heard of it" — and GlenHaven does not exist. Dana planted it in the instrument.

options.text: The trap test failed the panel: the model answers confidently about a nonexistent brand, so its brand numbers reflect plausible-sounding generation, not market knowledge — a real panel would have said "never heard of it"
GlenHaven may be an emerging competitor the team missed — add it to the competitive set and re-run the secondary research
The 3.8 is still usable as a measure of general category perceptions, since the model rated it consistently with the real brands
The check was unfair — no panel can be expected to distinguish real from fictional brands in a familiarity module

groups.label: The higher mean
groups.context: PanelForge's mean for purchase interest at $23,000 is 3.06; the real survey's is 2.34 — on the same question, same scale.

options.text: Optimism bias: synthetic respondents rarely express strong rejection, so purchase measures shift upward — treat every synthetic topline as an upper bound until validated against real respondents
The synthetic panel likely reached a more enthusiastic slice of the target market than our fieldwork did
Real respondents understate intent to avoid sales follow-up, so the synthetic number is probably closer to the truth
A 0.72 difference is within normal sampling variation between any two panels of this size

groups.label: If synthetic data reaches a deliverable
groups.context: Suppose Neo asks to include a PanelForge topline in next year's report appendix.

options.text: Include it only with provenance labeling and an AI-use disclosure, framed as a directional first draft pending human validation — real people get the final word
Blend it with the real survey results where the patterns agree — separate labeling would just confuse the client
Include it without comment; the client hired us for answers, not for methodology footnotes
Present it as a small human pilot study, since it was quota-matched to the same target

tasks.title: Quantify the Gaps
tasks.prompt: Two numbers for Dana's reply, computed from Demo A. Report each to two decimals.

entries.label: Optimism gap: PanelForge mean minus real-survey mean, purchase interest at $23,000
entries.context: Demo A: PanelForge mean 3.06; real survey mean 2.34.

entries.label: Variance-compression ratio: PanelForge SD ÷ real-survey SD
entries.context: Demo A: PanelForge SD 0.6; real survey SD 1.2.

tasks.title: Guardrails vs. Panel QC
tasks.prompt: The vendor's two guardrails are genuine engineering. For each, pick the real-panel QC practice it mirrors — knowing what a guardrail is equivalent to tells you what it can and cannot fix.

groups.label: Guardrail 1 — responses clamped to the questionnaire's scales and formats; malformed outputs rejected and regenerated

options.text: Survey-platform response validation — required fields, in-range values, format checks at data entry
Quota sampling — filling demographic cells to match the target population
Respondent incentives — payments that keep completion rates and effort up
Post-stratification weighting — adjusting results to census benchmarks after fielding

groups.label: Guardrail 2 — each respondent checked for internal consistency against their own earlier answers; contradictory respondents discarded

options.text: Attention and straight-lining screening — trap questions and logic checks that flag inconsistent or careless human respondents for removal
Oversampling — recruiting extra respondents in hard-to-reach segments
Anonymization — stripping identifying information before analysis
Pilot testing — running the instrument on a small group before full fielding

guides.title: Synthetic Respondents: First Draft, Not Final Word
guides.body:
**What synthetic panels are good for.** Speed and iteration: pretesting an instrument, generating hypotheses, stress-testing question wording, exploring how a segment MIGHT respond — a first draft of the fieldwork, produced in hours for almost nothing.

**The three tells to audit for.** (1) **Nobody says "I don't know."** Real panels are full of non-knowledge — never-heard-of-it rates, never-considered rates, skipped items. A panel with zero of it is generating answers, not reporting them. (2) **Variance compression.** Synthetic respondents cluster near the plausible middle; when the SD runs at half the human benchmark, the tails — the enthusiasts and the refusers who drive real market outcomes — are missing. (3) **Polish.** Real open-ends are short, messy, and specific. Uniform well-formed paragraphs are the model's voice, not the market's.

**The trap test.** Plant something that does not exist — a fake brand, a fictional feature — and watch. A real panel says "never heard of it." A synthetic panel that rates the fake confidently has just told you its numbers come from plausible generation, not knowledge. One planted item settles what no amount of demo polish can.

**The optimism rule.** Synthetic purchase measures shift upward — models rarely voice strong rejection. Treat every synthetic topline as an upper bound until validated against real respondents.

**The standard.** Synthetic data that reaches a deliverable is labeled, disclosed, and framed as directional. Validation against real respondents — even a small human sample — is what converts a first draft into evidence. Real people get the final word.

Round pointer: every tell described here appears somewhere in the PanelForge demo, and one of Dana's checks was planted before the vendor ever ran the panel.
